mcqs.question: A fraud model trained on 1% positive data reports 99% accuracy but catches almost no actual fraud. What does this indicate?
options: The model is performing extremely well and is ready for production
The model must have a bug in its loss function implementation
The training data needs more features to fix this
Accuracy is misleading here — the model likely learned to predict the majority class almost always, and recall/precision should be checked instead
mcqs.explanation: With 99% of data in one class, predicting that class alone yields 99% accuracy while providing zero value for detecting fraud — the actual goal. This is a metric-choice problem, not a bug or a missing-feature problem; recall, precision, F1, or PR-AUC reveal what accuracy hides.

mcqs.question: A trained model ranks positives above negatives reasonably well (good AUC), but using the default 0.5 threshold gives poor recall on the rare positive class. What's the most direct fix?
options: Lower the decision threshold based on the precision/recall trade-off you need, without retraining
Retrain the entire model from scratch with a different algorithm
Discard the model since a good AUC with poor recall is contradictory
Apply SMOTE to the test set to rebalance it
mcqs.explanation: A good AUC means the model ranks predictions well; a poor recall at 0.5 just means the default cutoff doesn't match your goals. Threshold moving fixes this without retraining. Retraining or switching algorithms is unnecessary extra cost, the situation isn't contradictory, and resampling the test set would corrupt your evaluation.

mcqs.question: A team applies SMOTE to the entire dataset, then splits into train and test. Validation metrics look excellent but production performance is much worse. What went wrong?
options: SMOTE always overestimates performance regardless of when it's applied
Synthetic training points may have been interpolated using real minority points that ended up in the test set, leaking test information into training
The test set was too small to be reliable
SMOTE should never be used for fraud-style problems
mcqs.explanation: Applying SMOTE before the split lets synthetic training rows draw on real minority points now sitting in the test set, so the model has effectively seen fragments of test data during training — classic leakage. It's the ordering that's wrong, not SMOTE itself or the test set's size, and SMOTE is a legitimate tool for exactly this kind of problem when applied correctly.

mcqs.question: Lowering a fraud model's threshold from 0.3 to 0.1 increases fraud caught from 80 to 90 cases ($200 saved each) but increases false positives from 400 to 2,000 ($10 cost each). Should the threshold be lowered?
options: Yes, because catching more fraud cases is always the priority regardless of false positives
No, because the additional false-positive cost ($20,000 total at 0.1) exceeds the total fraud savings ($18,000), making 0.1 a worse net outcome than 0.3 ($16,000 saved vs $4,000 cost)
Yes, because a lower threshold always improves F1 score
It cannot be determined without knowing the model's AUC
mcqs.explanation: Direct cost comparison: at threshold 0.1, $18,000 saved against $20,000 in false-positive costs is a net loss, while at 0.3, $16,000 saved against $4,000 cost is a clear net gain — so 0.3 is the better threshold here despite catching less fraud. Chasing maximum fraud caught or F1 alone ignores the actual asymmetric costs, and AUC (a ranking-quality metric) doesn't substitute for this specific threshold decision.

mcqs.question: A model shows a wildly different F1 score across the 5 folds of a plain random k-fold cross-validation on a 0.5%-positive dataset. What's the most likely fix?
options: Increase the number of folds to 20 without changing the splitting method
Switch to stratified k-fold splitting, which preserves the class ratio in each fold and prevents some folds from having too few (or zero) positive examples
Ignore F1 and only look at accuracy across folds instead
This instability is expected and cannot be fixed by changing the splitting method
mcqs.explanation: Plain random splitting can leave some folds with very few positives purely by chance on a rare-class problem, producing noisy per-fold metrics; stratified k-fold directly addresses this by keeping each fold's class ratio close to the overall dataset's. Simply adding more folds without stratifying doesn't fix the underlying cause, switching to accuracy would hide the real problem rather than solve it, and this instability is very much addressable by choosing the right splitting method.
